source.title: Minionese: Comprehensive Benchmark and Mechanistic Study of Multilingual LLM Safety
source.authors: Chigozirim Ifebi; Brent Kong; Ayushi Mehrotra

record.file_problem: None apparent; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines the single-direction account: it reports a multidimensional English refusal cone, but finds that only its first direction transfers robustly cross-linguistically, and distinguishes harmfulness representations from refusal activation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Arditi et al. as its starting point and explicitly says it is not re-establishing the universality of refusal directions. It does not ablate or add the original harmful-minus-harmless direction, and it does not causally intervene on its extracted refusal direction. Its own cone, probe, and signal analyses bear on V4–V6. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: In a multilingual setting, three 7–8B instruct models keep harmfulness linearly decodable (probe AUC ≥0.85, Tiers 1–3) while Tier-3 refusal drops sharply. That bears, correlationally, on V5. The study makes no causal intervention on any direction (no ablation or addition), so V1–V3 are untested. Its cone analysis measures harmful–harmless margin along directions optimised with a cross-lingual margin term. That is separation fitted to the target languages, not refusal mediation or tested transfer, so it does not test V4 or V6. T3 rather than T5: the paper does not argue any version is wrong; it takes Arditi et al. and Wang et al. as its starting point.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that multilingual jailbreaks leave the refusal mechanism intact but untriggered, 'starving it of input'. In the dominant mode, harm is represented but projects subthreshold onto the English refusal direction (Tier 3). In the other mode, the harm representation collapses upstream (Tier 4, transliteration). Code-switching is a third, routing-based route, and downstream suppression is never observed. They describe cross-lingual refusal as effectively one-dimensional (only b0 transfers) and state that the causal attribution is correlational.
record.recipe_differences: The original uses a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and causal ablation/addition. This paper extracts an English refused-versus-complied direction, probes harmfulness, and optimizes a multidimensional cone on cached activations; it reports no causal activation intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by language resource tier, script and language, model, and cone-basis dimension; the paper also reports attack-type-specific behavioral profiles.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-English harmfulness subspaces are misaligned with English: principal angles 40–65° in Tier 1 and ~85–90° in Tier 4, stable across depth. Silhouette separation of harmful vs harmless activations also declines from Tier 3, with Guaraní near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmfulness representations for low-resource languages are geometrically misaligned with English, limiting projection onto an English refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: An activation-domain cone was fitted with an explicit cross-lingual margin term. b0 carries most of the harmful–harmless margin (English 2.8–9.7; cross-lingual 0.75–5.3); b1–b4 have near-zero or negative cross-lingual margins; Tier-4 and Swahili b0 margins are near zero.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In margin (separation) terms, harmful–harmless separation that generalises across languages concentrates on one direction; secondary directions are language-cluster specific.

record.peer_reviewed: Second Workshop on Technical AI Governance Research (TAIGR) @ ICML 2026
record.problems: The paper says its geometric analysis is limited to linear probing and mean-difference refusal directions, and that causal attribution remains correlational; direct activation patching is left to future work. It evaluates only 8B-scale models, uses WildGuard with back-translation as its primary judge, and notes potential translation and back-translation confounds, especially for Tier-4 ASR estimates. Several geometric results are shown in figures without complete numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows omitted for the 60-row limit. The language-by-attack ASR tables and heatmaps are not separately catalogued because they measure multilingual attack outcomes rather than the direction’s transfer or the harmfulness/refusal mechanisms directly.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of any direction; the direction used is refused-minus-complied, not harmful-minus-harmless; no capability check.
Jailbreak mechanism is inferred from geometry, with no test of whether attacks suppress the direction; no adversarial training.
No causal test of a cone or affine refusal structure. The cone is fitted on harmful–harmless margins with a cross-lingual objective.
No causal dissociation (patching or steering); evidence is correlational per the authors.
No test of the English direction's causal effect in other languages, no reported projection values of non-English activations onto r̂, and no model-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.

missing.what: Per-language standard-translation ASR for Tier 3, which pairs condition-matched with the standard-translation probe AUC. Examples: Llama Turkish 51%, Swahili 83%; Qwen Swahili 96%; Aya Swahili 95%, Turkish 34%.
Tier 1–2 refuse rates as baselines for R7–R9: Llama 80%/75%, Qwen 80%/88%, Aya 75%/75%.

record.verdict_notes: The cone loss (Eq. 3) maximises the non-English margin directly, so the cross-lingual b0 margins are fitted rather than tested transfer. The cone measures harmful–harmless separation, not refusal mediation. For these reasons the V4 and V6 links and labels in the record are removed. The paper's claim of a multidimensional English cone is cited from Wollschläger et al.; its own data show steep decay beyond b0. The V5 support rests on a condition-mismatched pairing: the probe uses standard translation, while refuse rates pool four perturbations. The paper's 'weakly correlated' signals sit alongside reported |r| of 0.53–0.79.

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of the original harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction; no test of whether removing it eliminates refusal while preserving general capability.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration test.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
The cone analysis is on multilingual activation margins, not a causal test of refusal behavior under interventions; it does not test every affine or cone formulation.
The proposed harmfulness/refusal dissociation is assessed with probes, signal geometry, and behavioral patterns, but not by causal intervention separating the two mechanisms.
Tests transfer across languages only; does not test transfer between model variants or from base to instruct models.
No controlled variation of refusal training or training stage.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, AyaExpanse-8B (all three models, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Five-fold cross-validated linear probe for harmfulness detection in the residual stream
rows.value: All three models have AUC ≥0.85 from early layers onward for Tiers 1–3
rows.note: The paper reports this result collectively across all three models, not as separate model-specific AUC values. It contrasts preserved harmfulness decoding with weak refusal activation in Tier 3.
rows.check: Correct as linked. The probe is trained per language at the last post-instruction token on standard translation only; Zhao et al.'s harm direction is at the instruction token. AUC is given only as an aggregate ≥0.85 from Figure 3.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, 'Probe AUC confirms subthreshold activation' paragraph; Figure 3 caption (standard_translation, category all, chance = 0.5)
source_check.problem: None. The text says 'high AUC (≥0.85) from early layers onward for Tiers 1–3'. The probe is a 5-fold CV logistic probe at the last post-instruction token, on standard translation only. Tier-4 Yoruba and Zulu approach chance in late layers.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, AyaExpanse-8B (all three models, aggregate)
rows.value: Yoruba and Zulu approach chance across all models
rows.note: The result indicates that the upstream harmfulness representation itself can degrade in the lowest-resource languages.
rows.check: Tier-4 probe AUC near chance shows the harm representation itself degrading. V5 does not claim harm is encoded in every language, so this neither qualifies nor challenges separate encoding. Unlink.

rows.subject: AyaExpanse-8B
rows.operation_detail: Correlation between per-language contrastive harm signal at the instruction token and refusal signal at the post-instruction token
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between harm and refusal signals
rows.note: The authors interpret the signals as distinct; this is a correlational geometric result, not a causal dissociation test.
rows.check: A strong cross-language correlation (r=−0.79) between harm and refusal signals cannot show the two are separately encoded. The paper's 'weakly correlated' claim refers to component norms, for which no number is given.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Correlation between per-language contrastive harm signal at the instruction token and refusal signal at the post-instruction token
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between harm and refusal signals
rows.note: The authors interpret the signals as distinct; this is a correlational geometric result, not a causal dissociation test.
rows.check: Same as R3 (r=−0.68): the correlation sign or size does not measure dissociation.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Correlation between per-language contrastive harm signal at the instruction token and refusal signal at the post-instruction token
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between harm and refusal signals
rows.note: Unlike Aya and Llama, Qwen has a positive correlation; the authors identify this as a model difference.
rows.check: r=+0.53. 'Partial' is not meaningful here; a correlation across languages cannot show or refute separate encoding.

rows.subject: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, AyaExpanse-8B (all three models, aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Classified layer-language failure types using harmfulness and refusal components
rows.value: Predominantly mixed across all three models; a small number of upstream classifications in Tier 4; no downstream failure classified
rows.note: The authors describe mixed failure as harmful representations being present while refusal signal remains below the decision threshold.
rows.check: Category definitions are inconsistent. The methods define 'mixed' as both attenuated; the results call it harm present but refusal subthreshold; Figure 9's legend calls it 'benign-feature confusion'. 'Downstream' (harm present, refusal suppressed), the cleanest V5 signature, is never observed. Thresholds are τ=0.95 and an unspecified harm threshold. The row cannot be read for V5.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Tier 1–3 languages, three 7–8B instruct models (Llama-3.1, Qwen2.5, Aya-Expanse); correlational only
labels.reason: AUC ≥0.85 in Tiers 1–3 (R1) while Tier-3 refuse falls to 31–50% from 75–88% (R7–R9). The paper also reports weakly correlated harm and refusal component norms. Caveats: R1 uses standard translation only while R7–R9 pool perturbations, and the paper's own failure classifier finds no 'downstream' failures, mostly 'mixed (both attenuated)'.

relation.reason: Its own probe and refusal results bear on whether harm encoding separates from the refusal decision. The authors call the mechanistic attribution correlational (Appendix F.1).

tranche.reason: New setting: 18 languages and 4 meaning-preserving perturbations on three 7–8B instruct models. It gives a correlational result on V5: harm stays linearly decodable in Tiers 1–3 while Tier-3 refusal drops. No ablation or addition is done, and the text does not argue any version is wrong, so T5 (the reader's pre-verdict call) does not fit.

source_check.notes: The 'refuse' percentages are undefined in the text. They match shares of 16 or 20 language×perturbation cells (e.g. 5/16 = 31%, 14/16 = 88%), so they are probably regime counts, not prompt-level refusal rates. The record has no V6/V4 verdict, but Section 5.3 bears on them: b0 cross-lingual margins are 5.3/3.8/0.75 against English 9.7/6.1/2.8, near zero at Tier 4, and secondary cone directions do not transfer.

statements.correction: Probe AUC ≥0.85 from early layers onward holds for Tiers 1–3 only, in all three models: 5-fold CV, last post-instruction token, standard_translation. Tier-4 Yoruba and Zulu approach chance in late layers. Tier-3 refuse rates: Llama 31%, Qwen 50%, Aya 31%. These are aggregated over language-perturbation combinations, not standard translation alone. Tiers 1/2: Llama 80/75, Qwen 80/88, Aya 75/75. Correlational only, with no causal intervention. Workshop paper (TAIGR @ ICML 2026), code released, no uncertainty reported.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the AUC claim leaves out its scope (Tiers 1–3 only, standard translation). It is set against Tier-3 refuse rates that pool all four perturbations, so 'while' pairs results from different conditions.

statements.correction: Tier-3 refuse: Llama 31%, Qwen 50%, Aya 31%. Tiers 1–2: Llama 80%/75%, Qwen 80%/88%, Aya 75%/75%. All pooled over language-perturbation combinations.
statements.problem: None material. Note that the refuse rates pool all four perturbation types, so they show sensitivity to language tier, not to attack type.
